htb-active.title: Discover the available services
htb-active.context: Active connects SMB access with information from a Windows domain. You can use Nmap to build an initial picture of reachable ports before examining what a particular service exposes.
htb-active.why: A port response is a clue about an available service. It does not by itself prove that the service is vulnerable or that anonymous access is allowed.

htb-active.title: Understand offline candidate testing
htb-active.context: The reading connects exposed credentials with Kerberoasting. Explore Hashcat's candidate-testing model as background for the related idea of offline password recovery.
htb-active.why: A candidate is checked using the target's format and parameters. A successful comparison identifies a candidate that satisfies that check; it does not reverse a hash into readable text.

htb-bashed.title: Connect writable files to execution privileges
htb-bashed.context: Bashed moves from a web shell to delegated permissions and writable scripts. Follow the animation as a reminder to connect what the current account can change with the account that later executes it.
htb-bashed.why: Write permission alone does not mean elevated access. The important relationship is whether a more privileged process trusts or runs something the current account can influence.

htb-blue.title: Turn a service response into a question
htb-blue.context: Nmap is one of Blue's listed topics. Use this visual beside the SMB enumeration discussion, then follow the article's evidence about the Windows service and its patch status.
htb-blue.why: An open port identifies somewhere to investigate. Vulnerability evidence is a separate finding; a service being reachable does not alone establish that it can be exploited.

htb-devel.title: Separate initial access from higher privileges
htb-devel.context: Devel connects files uploaded through FTP with execution by a web service, then discusses missing Windows patches. This visual belongs with the later question of which privileges become available after initial access.
htb-devel.why: Running code and running it with administrative permissions are different conditions. A local weakness can matter because it lets a process move beyond the permissions it started with.

htb-jerry.title: Find a service before studying its features
htb-jerry.context: Jerry introduces scanning before examining Tomcat management and application deployment. You can use Nmap to understand the service discovery stage shown here.
htb-jerry.why: A network scan helps locate reachable services. Understanding the management interface and its authentication requires further investigation beyond the port result.

htb-lame.title: Keep more than one service hypothesis
htb-lame.context: Lame compares an unsuccessful FTP route with a later Samba investigation. Nmap is a related discovery tool that can help you organize the services available for closer investigation.
htb-lame.why: A discovered service is a starting point for a question. When a proposed route fails, observations from other services can support a different hypothesis.

htb-legacy.title: Gather evidence about the older service
htb-legacy.context: Legacy starts with SMB discovery before vulnerability validation and tooling compatibility. You can use the Nmap visual to understand the discovery step without assuming every detected service is vulnerable.
htb-legacy.why: The response tells you something about reachability from your scanning position. Matching a vulnerability or tool to an older system needs additional evidence.

htb-nibbles.title: Read a script's permissions in context
htb-nibbles.context: Nibbles follows its web investigation with a discussion of script permissions and privilege escalation. At that point, connect the ability to change a script with the permissions under which it may run.
htb-nibbles.why: Sudo rules define which commands an account may run as another user. A permissive rule becomes especially significant when the permitted command or something it uses can be changed.

htb-optimum.title: Use service information to narrow the investigation
htb-optimum.context: Optimum begins with service version discovery around HTTP File Server. Nmap is a related tool for exploring reachable services before interpreting the version evidence described in the reading.
htb-optimum.why: Discovery narrows what to examine next. A reported service version still needs interpretation alongside the actual environment and observed behavior.

htb-optimum.title: Recheck the conditions after initial access
htb-optimum.context: Optimum treats initial access and local Windows privilege escalation as separate decisions. Use the animation at the later stage to follow the change from the current account's permissions to higher privileges.
htb-optimum.why: The conditions that permit a network entry point are not automatically the conditions needed for local elevation. The current account and local system state determine what can happen next.

htb-shocker.title: Follow the permission granted by sudo
htb-shocker.context: Shocker moves from the CGI and Shellshock investigation to a permissive sudo rule. This animation belongs with that final permissions discussion.
htb-shocker.why: A sudo rule grants a particular way to run a command as another user. Understanding what that command can do explains why the rule can change the account's effective capabilities.

htb-valentine.title: Distinguish finding a key from unlocking it
htb-valentine.context: Valentine explicitly connects an encrypted SSH key with other clues. The cipher vault illustrates why obtaining an encrypted file and being able to use its protected contents are separate steps.
htb-valentine.why: Encryption protects readable data using a key. An SSH private key can itself be stored under passphrase protection, so possessing that file does not necessarily make its contents immediately usable.

thm-rootme.title: Notice whose permissions a program uses
thm-rootme.context: RootMe moves from a limited web account to an investigation of SUID and Linux permissions. Follow the animation alongside that change in the account's available capabilities.
thm-rootme.why: An executable with SUID can run with its owner's effective user identity. Its behavior and configuration determine whether that permission can be used to cross an intended access boundary.

thm-pickle-rick.title: Look beyond the command panel's restrictions
thm-pickle-rick.context: Pickle Rick separates the command panel's filtering from the account's broad sudo permissions. This visual fits the later question of which privileges the underlying account can obtain.
thm-pickle-rick.why: Filtering selected input and limiting operating system privileges control different things. A sudo permission can grant capabilities that the visible command panel does not make obvious.

thm-blue.title: Start with the service evidence
thm-blue.context: The Blue reading begins with a Windows service scan before selecting a vulnerability. Nmap is a related discovery tool; this visual explains how responses help build the initial service picture.
thm-blue.why: Discovery tells you where a service may be reachable. The later vulnerability assessment must establish more than the fact that a port responded.

thm-blue.title: Understand what a saved hash can be checked against
thm-blue.context: Password hashes appear later in Blue, after administrative access. Explore Hashcat as a related tool for testing password candidates against supported saved hashes.
thm-blue.why: A candidate is processed with the same format and relevant parameters as the target. Comparing the result can establish a match; merely possessing a hash does not reveal the password.

thm-blue.title: Compare another view of candidate testing
thm-blue.context: John the Ripper is another tool you can use to study offline password recovery with supported hash formats. Its animation provides a second view of the candidate-and-comparison idea related to Blue's password hash discussion.
thm-blue.why: The saved hash acts as a verifier rather than readable password text. Processing candidates in the corresponding format lets the tool test whether one matches that verifier.

thm-basic-pentesting.title: Build the service picture before following account clues
thm-basic-pentesting.context: Basic Pentesting begins with service discovery before user identification and password investigation. You can use Nmap to understand the initial discovery stage illustrated here.
thm-basic-pentesting.why: Knowing which services respond helps organize the next questions. A service response does not supply a valid username, password or private key by itself.

thm-basic-pentesting.title: See how password candidates are tested
thm-basic-pentesting.context: This reading lists password cracking and SSH keys among its topics. Explore John the Ripper as a related auditing tool for supported hashes and protected key formats.
thm-basic-pentesting.why: An offline password check compares a candidate's computed result with the saved target. Each unsuccessful candidate is another guess, and recovery depends on testing a candidate that satisfies the check.

thm-basic-pentesting.title: Explore candidate checks in parallel
thm-basic-pentesting.context: Hashcat offers another way to study offline password auditing for supported formats. This related visual shows multiple candidate checks in parallel beside Basic Pentesting's password cracking topic.
thm-basic-pentesting.why: Parallel work can test more candidates at once, but each candidate still has to satisfy the target's check. Faster testing helps cover the candidate set; it does not ensure the correct password is in that set.

thm-vulnversity.title: Notice the web service beyond the usual ports
thm-vulnversity.context: Nmap is explicitly listed in Vulnversity, where the reading highlights a web service beyond the default ports. This visual explains the scan-and-response idea behind that discovery.
thm-vulnversity.why: Applications can listen on ports other than the ones you first expect. A scan's scope matters because a service cannot be discovered through a port that was never checked.

thm-vulnversity.title: Connect the service manager to its effective permissions
thm-vulnversity.context: After the web upload investigation, Vulnversity examines SUID on a service manager. The elevation animation belongs with that operating system permissions discussion.
thm-vulnversity.why: SUID can make an executable run with its owner's effective user identity. Whether that becomes an unintended path to higher access depends on what the executable permits and how it is configured.
